messages.subject: Why should use multipleGroup?
parts:
# in this example, lets simulate some Rasch data so that we know whats going on
set.seed(1234)
nitems <- 15
d1 <- d2 <- matrix(rnorm(nitems,0,.7),ncol=1)
d2[1:3, ] <- d2[1:3, ] + c(.5, 1, 1.5)
d2[4:6, ] <- d2[4:6, ] - c(.5, 1, 1.5)
data.frame(d.group1 = d1, d.group2 = d2)

itemtype <- rep('dich', nitems)
N <- 500
dataset1 <- simdata(matrix(1,nitems), d1, N, itemtype)
dataset2 <- simdata(matrix(1,nitems), d2, N, itemtype, mu = .25, sigma = matrix(1.5))
dat <- rbind(dataset1, dataset2)
group <- c(rep('D1', N), rep('D2', N))

#get same result when use or not use multipleGroup
coef(multipleGroup(dat,1, group, itemtype = 'Rasch'), simplify=TRUE)
coef(mirt(dataset1,1,itemtype = 'Rasch'),simplify=TRUE)
coef(mirt(dataset2,1,itemtype = 'Rasch'),simplify=TRUE)

When we know the group,we can get mirt result based on each group.
I tested through above sample,get the same result as multipleGroup.

Then,what's the advantage of multipleGroup??

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Why should use multipleGroup?
parts:
Multiple group estimation allows you to constrain parameters to be equal across groups, as well as free the originally unidentifiable latent trait mean/variance parameters. This allows the groups to be equated so that you can test for DIF and such. The default you are seeing above is what is known as 'configural invariance', which assumes that the groups have the same mean/variance in the latent trait (a strong and usually incorrect assumption). HTH.

Phil
